agentCan: Implement the authorization code flow (Basic auth at the token endpoint, Bearer at the API) and the 24-hour-window refresh scheduling
Prepare the publishing form packet (integration details, images, marketing copy)

approval.cost: 'We don't charge any fees for publishing apps, and how you price your product is entirely up to you' (stated)
approval.trigger: Private apps: no review. 'By default, apps are private to the Front instance they are created in. Once you create an app, you do not need to take additional steps for it to be available to Front users in that instance.' Public/App Store distribution requires Front's approval via a manual, human process: 'If you want to make an app available for all Front customers to use, you must publish your app... To publish your app, notify our team.' You fill out a form with the requested details; 'We'll use your form submission to first test your integration and let you know if everything looks good. Once your integration has been technically approved, our team will use the image and marketing details you submit in the form to launch your integration with a dedicated landing page on our website and in our app.' Refusal grounds include security concerns or lack of transparency about who runs your company, integrations that do not run on the Front platform, poor integration quality, license-utilization integrations that may negatively impact Front revenue, and browser extensions (not published). 'Smaller teams may also be subject to a security or legal review.' Evaluation is 'on a case-by-case basis', though 'We are currently an open integration platform and approve the vast majority of integrations submitted to us.' No pre-approval numeric caps are stated; structurally, before publishing your app is only available inside the Front instance where it was created.
approval.wait: Not stated (no review duration or SLA anywhere in the docs read)

blockers.detail: 'Refresh tokens are valid for 6 months... During the six months of validity, the API will return the same refresh token to you when you obtain new tokens. In the last 24 hours of validity, however, the API will return a new refresh token, which will then start a new six month period of validity.' Refreshing regularly mid-window returns the SAME refresh token with the SAME original expiry date, so naive 'refresh daily' logic does not extend the connection; if you never refresh inside that final 24-hour window, the refresh token dies and the customer must redo the whole OAuth flow.
blockers.howToClear: Schedule a refresh inside the final 24 hours of each refresh token's validity, or accept periodic re-authorization.
blockers.title: The 6-month refresh clock only rolls over in its last 24 hours

blockers.detail: 'End users authorizing OAuth apps must be admins. This applies to both private and public OAuth apps.' A non-admin champion at a customer cannot complete the connect flow. (The sole exception is Front's own MCP server connection, which uses user-scoped tokens any teammate can authorize.)
blockers.howToClear: Tell customers up front that a Front admin must perform the connection.
blockers.title: Only an admin can connect a customer

blockers.detail: 'Once your app is published to all customers, you cannot make direct changes to it. Instead, create a new app to test your changes, and then notify us using the email thread created when we first published your app.'
blockers.howToClear: Plan on parallel app versions for public integrations from the start.
blockers.title: Published apps are frozen

alternatives: API tokens (company-level Bearer tokens created under Settings > Developers > API Tokens tab, admins only; Front positions them for 'building an integration for your own Front instance or a single Front customer', and warns: 'Front requires that partners implement OAuth instead of API tokens when building Core API integrations that make updates on behalf of a Front customer or their account, unless you obtain an exception from us')
flavor.recommended: An app on the Front Platform with the OAuth feature enabled, using the authorization code grant (the only grant Front supports)
flavor.why: OAuth is not a separate registration; it is a feature you add to an app: Features tab > Add feature > OAuth > Enable OAuth, which reveals the Client ID and Client secret, lets you register redirect URLs, and is where you configure the features, namespaces, and permissions the token will carry. Front's position: 'In general, Front recommends implementing OAuth when feasible', and 'we require that partner integrations connect to the Core API via OAuth unless you obtain an exception from us. The only exceptions we currently consider are ones where you cannot access certain Front resources via OAuth.' Scopes are NOT passed at authorize time: they are the app-level configuration (features like Core API resources; namespaces: global/shared/private; permissions per resource: Read, Write, Delete, Send).

humanMust: (Partners) Sign up for a free development account
Create the app in Front's UI (name, short description, icon all display to end users) and enable the OAuth feature
Configure features, namespaces, and permissions on the OAuth feature
For public launch: submit the publishing form and correspond with Front's team
name: Front
nuances: Token-endpoint auth differs from API auth: token requests use HTTP Basic (Base64 client_id:client_secret) against app.frontapp.com, while all other API calls use Bearer against api2.frontapp.com. 'Basic authentication is only used when making OAuth requests to the https://app.frontapp.com/ OAuth service.' The redirect_uri in the token exchange 'MUST be the same URL as the one used in the step to request an authorization code'.

For a token to touch a teammate's private resources (personal inboxes, signatures), 'the teammate will have to enable API access in their settings', an extra per-teammate switch outside the OAuth consent.

Feature asymmetry between token types: Application triggers are 'not currently available for OAuth tokens', while the MCP server feature is 'not available for API tokens'; the auth method you choose forecloses some functionality either way. SCIM/Auto-provisioning 'you have to contact our team to learn more about (not generally available to the public)'.
Access tokens expire in 60 minutes; refresh is triggered by a 401 from the API. The token response includes expires_at rather than a bare expires_in.

API token gotchas: tokens are company-level (visible to all admins, not tied to a user, so access survives staff changes but cannot be attributed to a person); the value 'cannot view it after creation'; deletion 'will immediately prevent any applications using the token from making requests... this operation cannot be undone'.
prerequisites: A Front account (a free development account is recommended for partners)
App name, short description, and icon (all public-facing)
Redirect URLs to register on the OAuth feature

steps.detail: 'If you don't already have an account, you'll want to sign up for a free development account' rather than testing on production data.
steps.title: (Partners) Get a development account

steps.detail: Settings > Company > Developers > Create app: App name and Short description, edit the icon, Save. 'The app name, short description, and icon display to end users of your app.'
steps.title: Create the app

steps.detail: Open the app > Features tab > Add feature > OAuth > Enable OAuth. Note the Client ID and Client secret, click Add Redirect URL (multiple allowed; 'Front recommends you delete your development URLs once your app is live'), and specify the features, namespaces, and permissions users will authorize.
steps.title: Enable OAuth; register redirect URLs; configure permissions

steps.detail: GET app.frontapp.com/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id={clientId}&redirect_uri={redirectURI} (optional state for CSRF protection). The authorizing user must be an admin. On acceptance Front redirects to your redirect URI with code and state; if the states don't match, 'you should consider the request as insecure and the process should be aborted'.
steps.title: Redirect the (admin) user to authorize

steps.detail: POST app.frontapp.com/oauth/token with code, redirect_uri (must be the same URL as the authorize step), grant_type=authorization_code, authenticated with HTTP Basic auth (Base64 client_id:client_secret). Response: access_token, refresh_token, expires_at, token_type Bearer. 'Please store the refresh_token securely.' Call the Core API (api2.frontapp.com) with Authorization: Bearer.
steps.title: Exchange the code (Basic auth); call the Core API

steps.detail: Access tokens expire in 60 minutes (the API returns 401). POST the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token and Basic auth, and store the new token set. Critically, refresh inside the LAST 24 HOURS of the refresh token's 6-month validity to receive a new refresh token and start a new 6-month period.
steps.title: Refresh (and mind the 24-hour rollover window)

steps.detail: Fill out Front's publishing form with the requested details. Front tests your integration; once technically approved, they launch it with a dedicated landing page and an in-product App Store listing. 'We don't charge any fees for publishing apps.'
steps.title: (Public launch) Submit for publishing

tagline: App-platform OAuth, authorization-code only: private apps in your own Front instance need no approval, but App Store publishing takes a manual, form-based technical approval from Front's team (no fee, no stated timeline), and refresh tokens only extend if you refresh inside their final 24 hours.

time.active: ~20 min of app setup + ~1-2 hrs of flow code
time.total: Same day for private apps; public publishing duration not stated
